The DHSC Office for Health Improvement and Disparities produce around 60-80 official statistics products per year covering all topics on public health, these are in the form of health profiles on our Fingertips platform, bespoke reports and analysis or through some of the 1,500 indicators of health published via the Fingertips platform.  https://fingertips.phe.org.uk which provide a valued resource for public health professionals.

DHSC use datasets provided under this agreement to generate intelligence to support local health professionals and others in the wider health and care system to rapidly responding to local enquiries and providing training on their use.  Examples of use of intelligence produced include:

1.	Major Conditions - Liver disease profiles
Liver disease is one of the main causes of premature mortality nationally. The profiles are designed to support local authorities by providing dataintelligence in a user-friendly format to allow them to assess the effect of liver disease in their areas and take action to prevent it. Data are presented by upper tier local authority, former Government Office Region, and England. Lower tier local authority level data are also presented, where available.  HES Is the key sources of data for this profile.

2. Excess Mortality in England and English Regions
https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/excess-mortality-in-england-and-english-regions
Identifiable data has been is used to link HES data to a number of datasets (e.g. ONS mortality data, COVID19 test results, Vaccination data, GPES) both to enrich theses datasets with ethnic category, add other data items where they are missing in the datasets, and to investigate the impact of COVID19 on factors such as mortality rates, hospital admissions, life expectancy and disparities. Identifiable data is only used to enable the linkage of these datasets, the analysis is carried out on a pseudonymised version (once linked).

DHSC have also been able to adjust for the impact of co-morbidities on survival from Covid-19 and therefore excess mortality.  This enables DHSC to more accurately estimate excess deaths, and to predict winter deaths to assist NHS England’s winter planning.

The analysis has identified the causes where DHSC have seen excess deaths in recent months, such as those with a mention of CVD or diabetes.  This is important for national clinical directors to know, and DHSC are also working further with the data to try to understand more about the drivers of this excess.  This information will help inform policy.  This analysis is used by Local authorities, the NHS, politicians and researchers to drive policy and planning as it shows trends in excess mortality by cause.  

3. Public Health Outcomes Framework
https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/public-health-outcomes-framework
The framework focuses on the two high level outcomes we want to achieve across the public health system and beyond:
1.  Increased healthy life expectancy
2.  Reduced differences in life expectancy and healthy life expectancy between communities

4. Premature mortality in adults with severe mental illness (SMI)
The SMI report is written for national organisations that lead and develop strategy, policy and guidance for the wellbeing of people with SMI;
local organisations that plan, manage and deliver preventive, clinical and supportive services for people with SMI;
local organisations that, along with mental health services, diagnose and treat physical health conditions in people with SMI and support them to live better with these conditions.
This work reveals the extent of geographical and deprivation inequalities in premature mortality in people with SMI, i.e. shows where is need greatest. It highlights that action is needed to tackle this significant inequality, provides some detail on what to address, and also offers an annual set of metrics that assess if actions are making a difference.
The data is provided to help local areas understand the needs of their population and to assess if the interventions they put in place are helping to reduce premature mortality in the population with SMI.

5. Drug and Alcohol work programme - BOLD

Mental health services are typically provided through the NHS, whereas drug and alcohol services are often provided by third sector or private organisations. Identifiers are needed to link records from NDTMS to MHSDS to enable the identification of people who are receiving treatment from third or private sector drug and alcohol services (NDTMS) who are also in contact with secondary mental health services (MHSDS). This will allow DHSC to differentiate between people receiving treatment for a substance use disorder only compared to those receiving treatment for co-occurring substance use and mental health disorders.

Both alcohol dependence and mental ill-health alone are associated with a range of adverse health outcomes for individuals, however, experiencing these issues concurrently, means people are even more likely to develop physical conditions related to alcohol. Despite evidence showing how frequently mental health and harmful drinking co-occur, and increased mortality in this group, people with co-occurring problems do not always receive coordinated support to address their needs. Current guidance describes three treatment models for co-occurring problems: serial (receive treatment for each problem, one service at a time), parallel (both problems are addressed by separate services at the same time), and integrated (one service addresses both problems in the same time and setting). Despite these guidelines, sometimes people only seek treatment for one problem (i.e., if that is causing more of an issue than the co-occurring problem), or long gaps between serial treatments mean that people only ever receive help for one problem. This linkage to data provided through this agreement generates novel and important epidemiological data to understand the extent to which having a mental health treatment need impacts successful completion of treatment within drug and alcohol services, and the types of treatment pathways that people with co-occurring problems are routinely provided, and whether different treatment pathways are associated with patient outcomes. All this helps to plan future service improvement/redesign.
